source.text: וַיְהִי֙ אַחֲרֵי־כֵ֔ן וַיָּ֕מָת נָחָ֖שׁ מֶ֣לֶךְ בְּנֵי־עַמּ֑וֹן וַיִּמְלֹ֥ךְ בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was after thus, and died Nahash king of [the] sons of Ammon, and reigned his son in his place.

en.L: And it happened after this that Nahash the king of the sons of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his place.
en.B: Some time after this, Nahash king of the Ammonites died, and his son became king in his place.
en.R: Some time later, Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, died, and his son became the new king.

decisions.choice: 1 Chronicles 19:1-19 retells 2 Samuel 10:1-19
decisions.reason: This chapter follows 2 Samuel 10 closely, and each record notes where its words differ. Chronicles leaves out David's kindness to Saul's grandson Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9), so here "after this" follows the summary of David's wars in chapter 18. In this verse Chronicles names the king who died, Nahash, and does not name his son until verse 2; 2 Samuel 10:1 names the son, Hanun, and leaves the father's name to its verse 2.

decisions.choice: after this: a loose link to what comes before, not a date
decisions.reason: The phrase opens a new story without saying how long after the events before it this happened. Chapter 18 has already summed up David's victories, among them his wars with Aram and the silver he took from Ammon (18:3-11); this chapter tells how the war with Ammon and its Aramean allies began.

decisions.choice: Nahash king of the Ammonites
decisions.reason: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan, with its capital at Rabbah (20:1). Nahash had besieged Jabesh-gilead in the days of Saul (1 Samuel 11:1-11).

decisions.choice: the sons of Ammon (Literal); the Ammonites (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Sons of Ammon" is the usual Hebrew name for the people of Ammon. Literal keeps the phrase; Balanced and Readable use the people's name, as throughout this chapter and 2 Samuel 10.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜יד אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־חֶ֣סֶד׀עִם־חָנ֣וּן בֶּן־נָחָ֗שׁ כִּֽי־עָשָׂ֨ה אָבִ֤יו עִמִּי֙ חֶ֔סֶד וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח דָּוִ֛יד מַלְאָכִ֖ים לְנַחֲמ֣וֹ עַל־אָבִ֑יו וַיָּבֹאוּ֩ עַבְדֵ֨י דָוִ֜יד אֶל־אֶ֧רֶץ בְּנֵי־עַמּ֛וֹן אֶל־חָנ֖וּן לְנַחֲמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said David, I will do chesed with Hanun son of Nahash, because did his father with me chesed; and sent David messengers to comfort him concerning his father; and came [the] servants of David to [the] land of [the] sons of Ammon to Hanun to comfort him.

en.L: And David said, "I will deal [in] steadfast love with Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father dealt [in] steadfast love with me." So David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the sons of Ammon, to Hanun, to comfort him.
en.B: David said, "I will show faithful love to Hanun son of Nahash, because his father showed faithful love to me." So David sent messengers to console Hanun over the death of his father. And David's officials came to Hanun in the land of the Ammonites to console him.
en.R: David said, "Hanun's father Nahash showed faithful love to me. So I will show faithful love to his son Hanun." David sent messengers to comfort Hanun because his father had died. David's officials went to Hanun in the land of the Ammonites to comfort him.

decisions.choice: chesed: loyal kindness between allies
decisions.reason: Chesed is love that keeps faith within a bond (1 Samuel 20:8). Between two kings it is the loyalty of friends or treaty partners: Nahash had been good to David, and David means to keep up the friendship with his son. The same word is used of God's own love (Exodus 34:6).

decisions.choice: three small differences from 2 Samuel 10:2
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:2 says "just as his father showed chesed to me"; Chronicles says "because" he did, giving David's reason. Samuel says David sent "by the hand of his servants"; Chronicles says he sent "messengers", and then calls them David's servants. Chronicles also adds at the end that they came "to Hanun, to comfort him". The event is the same.

decisions.choice: because his father showed chesed to me: a kindness the Scriptures do not describe
decisions.reason: The text never says what Nahash had done for David. Nahash had been Saul's enemy (1 Samuel 11), so he may have helped David while Saul was hunting him. Later, when David fled from Absalom, Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah brought him supplies (2 Samuel 17:27).

decisions.choice: sent to comfort him concerning his father: a formal embassy of condolence
decisions.reason: When a king died, friendly rulers sent envoys to mourn with his heir. Such a visit also confirmed that the friendship between the two kingdoms would go on under the new king.

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The word is rendered the same way throughout, as in Exodus 34:6 and 2 Samuel 10:2.

decisions.choice: servants (Literal); officials (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The servants of a king are his officials, here sent as envoys. Literal keeps "servants"; Balanced and Readable say "officials", as in 2 Samuel 10:2.

source.text: וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ שָׂרֵ֨י בְנֵי־עַמּ֜וֹן לְחָנ֗וּן הַֽמְכַבֵּ֨ד דָּוִ֤יד אֶת־אָבִ֨יךָ֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֥ח לְךָ֖ מְנַחֲמִ֑ים הֲלֹ֡א בַּ֠עֲבוּר לַחְקֹ֨ר וְלַהֲפֹ֤ךְ וּלְרַגֵּל֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ בָּ֥אוּ עֲבָדָ֖יו אֵלֶֽיךָ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] princes of [the] sons of Ammon to Hanun, [Is] honoring David your father in your eyes because he has sent to you comforters? [Is it] not in order to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land [that] have come his servants to you?

en.L: And the princes of the sons of Ammon said to Hanun, "Is David honoring your father in your eyes because he has sent comforters to you? Is it not in order to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land that his servants have come to you?"
en.B: But the Ammonite officials said to Hanun, "Do you really think David is honoring your father by sending men to comfort you? Have his officials not come to you to explore, to overthrow, and to spy out the land?"
en.R: But the leaders of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you really believe David sent these men to comfort you because he respects your father? No! His officials have come to look over the land and spy on it, so that he can conquer it."

decisions.choice: is David honoring your father in your eyes?: do you think he is?
decisions.reason: "In your eyes" means "in your opinion". The question expects the answer "no": the officials are telling Hanun not to believe that the visit is a mark of respect.

decisions.choice: is it not in order to ...?: a question that states what they believe
decisions.reason: The second question expects the answer "yes". The officials claim the envoys came as spies.

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 10:3
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:3 calls Hanun "their lord", speaks of "the city", lists the verbs as search, spy out and overthrow, and says "David has sent his servants". Chronicles leaves out "their lord", speaks of "the land", puts "overthrow" before "spy out", and says "his servants have come". The charge is the same: the envoys are spies.

decisions.choice: search, overthrow, spy out: scout the land in order to take it
decisions.reason: Together the three verbs say that the visit was a first step toward conquest; their order here is not a sequence of events. The fear was not far-fetched, since David had just conquered Moab, Aram and Edom (18:2-13).

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word names the chief men around a king. The three levels follow the wording settled for this word in Samuel and 2 Samuel 10:3.

decisions.choice: No! His officials have come to ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the second question into the statement it implies, so that young readers do not miss the point.

source.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח חָנ֜וּן אֶת־עַבְדֵ֤י דָוִיד֙ וַֽיְגַלְּחֵ֔ם וַיִּכְרֹ֧ת אֶת־מַדְוֵיהֶ֛ם בַּחֵ֖צִי עַד־הַמִּפְשָׂעָ֑ה וַֽיְשַׁלְּחֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And took Hanun [the] servants of David and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the middle as far as the buttocks, and sent them away.

en.L: So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the middle, as far as the buttocks, and sent them away.
en.B: So Hanun seized David's officials, shaved them, cut their garments off in the middle at the buttocks, and sent them on their way.
en.R: So Hanun took David's officials and shaved them. He cut their robes short, so that their backsides were left bare. Then he sent them away.

decisions.choice: shaved them: 2 Samuel 10:4 says he shaved off half of their beard
decisions.reason: Chronicles says only that Hanun shaved the men; 2 Samuel 10:4 says he shaved off half of each man's beard. The beard is meant here too, since in verse 5 David tells the men to wait until their beards grow back. Chronicles also uses a different and rare word for the buttocks, found only here; it names the same part of the body.

decisions.choice: shaving the envoys: a deliberate public insult
decisions.reason: A full beard was a mark of a grown man's honor. Men cut their beards only in deep mourning or disgrace (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 48:37). Shaving the envoys by force made them look ridiculous, and the insult fell on David, who had sent them.

decisions.choice: cutting their garments to the buttocks: stripping them like captives
decisions.reason: Long robes were the dress of men of standing. Cutting them off at the buttocks left the men exposed, the shame done to prisoners of war (Isaiah 20:4). To treat a king's envoys this way was to reject his friendship and amounted to a challenge to war.

decisions.choice: He cut their robes short, so that their backsides were left bare
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the cut did, which is the point of the insult, as in 2 Samuel 10:4.

source.text: וַיֵּלְכוּ֩ וַיַּגִּ֨ידוּ לְדָוִ֤יד עַל־הָֽאֲנָשִׁים֙ וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח לִקְרָאתָ֔ם כִּי־הָי֥וּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים נִכְלָמִ֣ים מְאֹ֑ד וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ שְׁב֣וּ בִֽירֵח֔וֹ עַ֛ד אֲשֶׁר־יְצַמַּ֥ח זְקַנְכֶ֖ם וְשַׁבְתֶּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And they went and told David about the men, and he sent to meet them, for were the men humiliated greatly. And said the king, Stay in Jericho until that grows your beard, and you will return.

en.L: And they went and told David about the men, and he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly humiliated. And the king said, "Stay in Jericho until your beard has grown, and [then] return."
en.B: When people came and told David what had happened to the men, he sent messengers to meet them, because the men were deeply ashamed. The king said, "Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then come home."
en.R: Some people went and told David what had happened to the men. So he sent messengers to meet them, because they were so ashamed. The king told them, "Wait in Jericho until your beards grow again. Then come home."

decisions.choice: they went and told David about the men: a fuller form of 2 Samuel 10:5
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:5 says only "they told David". Chronicles adds "they went" and "about the men". Neither book says who went; it may have been the envoys themselves or others who saw them. The king's words are the same in both books.

decisions.choice: greatly humiliated: publicly disgraced
decisions.reason: The word describes the shame of being dishonored in front of others, not only a private feeling of embarrassment.

decisions.choice: stay in Jericho: wait out of sight on the way home
decisions.reason: Jericho lay just west of the Jordan, on the road from Ammon up to Jerusalem. By waiting there the envoys were spared being seen in the capital until they looked like themselves again. David's care for them also shows that he took the insult as his own.

decisions.choice: people came (Balanced); some people went (Readable); he sent messengers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "they went" and "he sent". Balanced and Readable say who went and who was sent, which the verbs imply.

source.text: וַיִּרְאוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן כִּ֥י הִֽתְבָּאֲשׁ֖וּ עִם־דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח חָ֠נוּן וּבְנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן אֶ֣לֶף כִּכַּר־כֶּ֗סֶף לִשְׂכֹּ֣ר לָ֠הֶם מִן־אֲרַ֨ם נַהֲרַ֜יִם וּמִן־אֲרַ֤ם מַעֲכָה֙ וּמִצּוֹבָ֔ה רֶ֖כֶב וּפָרָשִֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: And saw [the] sons of Ammon that they had made themselves odious with David, and sent Hanun and [the] sons of Ammon a thousand talents of silver to hire for themselves from Aram-naharaim and from Aram-maacah and from Zobah chariots and horsemen.

en.L: And the sons of Ammon saw that they had made themselves a stench to David, and Hanun and the sons of Ammon sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire for themselves chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim and from Aram-maacah and from Zobah.
en.B: When the Ammonites saw that they had made themselves hateful to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent {{units:about 37 tons|1,000 talents}} of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah and Zobah.
en.R: The Ammonites knew that they had made David their enemy. So Hanun and the Ammonites sent {{units:about 37 tons|1,000 talents}} of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from northern Mesopotamia, Maacah and Zobah.

decisions.choice: made themselves a stench to David: turned David into an enemy
decisions.reason: To become a bad smell to someone is to become hateful to him (Genesis 34:30; 1 Samuel 27:12; 2 Samuel 10:6). The Ammonites knew war would follow.

decisions.choice: the forces hired differ from 2 Samuel 10:6
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:6 says the Ammonites hired 20,000 foot soldiers from the Arameans of Beth-rehob and of Zobah, the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and 12,000 men of Tob. Chronicles names Hanun as one of those who sent, gives the price, a thousand talents of silver, and says they hired chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah and Zobah; it does not name Beth-rehob or Tob. The two writers drew on different records or counted the forces differently.

decisions.choice: Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah and Zobah: Aramean lands to the north and northeast
decisions.reason: Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers", was the land of the upper Euphrates in northern Mesopotamia, where Nahor's family lived (Genesis 24:10) and from which Cushan-rishathaim came (Judges 3:8). Aram-maacah, or Maacah, lay near the Golan, east of the upper Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:14). Zobah was the kingdom of Hadadezer (18:3).

decisions.choice: a thousand talents of silver: an enormous sum
decisions.reason: A talent was the largest weight, about 75 pounds. A thousand talents of silver was a king's ransom; Menahem paid the same amount to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 15:19).

decisions.choice: about 37 tons (1,000 talents)
decisions.reason: A talent was about 75 pounds, so a thousand talents was about 75,000 pounds. Literal keeps the Hebrew unit; Balanced and Readable give the modern measure with the talent as the alternative, as in 2 Kings 15:19.

decisions.choice: northern Mesopotamia; Maacah (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable names Aram-naharaim by the region it was, as in Genesis 24:10, and calls Aram-maacah simply Maacah, as verse 7 does.

source.text: וַיִּשְׂכְּר֣וּ לָהֶ֡ם שְׁנַיִם֩ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים אֶ֜לֶף רֶ֗כֶב וְאֶת־מֶ֤לֶךְ מַעֲכָה֙ וְאֶת־עַמּ֔וֹ וַיָּבֹ֕אוּ וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ לִפְנֵ֣י מֵידְבָ֑א וּבְנֵ֣י עַמּ֗וֹן נֶאֶסְפוּ֙ מֵעָ֣רֵיהֶ֔ם וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ לַמִּלְחָמָֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And they hired for themselves thirty-two thousand chariot[s], and [the] king of Maacah and his people; and they came and camped before Medeba. And [the] sons of Ammon were gathered from their cities and came to the battle.

en.L: And they hired for themselves 32,000 chariots, and the king of Maacah and his people; and they came and camped before Medeba. And the sons of Ammon were gathered from their cities and came to the battle.
en.B: They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, and these came and camped near Medeba. The Ammonites also gathered from their cities and came out to fight.
en.R: They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army. These forces came and set up camp near the town of Medeba. The Ammonites also came together from their towns and got ready for battle.

decisions.choice: 32,000 chariots: chariot forces, a very large number
decisions.reason: The word means chariots or chariotry, the chariots with their crews and horses. The number is far beyond the chariot forces of any king of the time. The word for "thousand" may also name a military unit, as noted at Numbers 1, and numbers were easily miscopied.

decisions.choice: the king of Maacah and Medeba: compare 2 Samuel 10:6
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:6 says the king of Maacah brought 1,000 men; Chronicles says "his people" without a number. The forces Samuel lists add up to 33,000 men, close to the 32,000 here, so the two books may be counting the same army in different ways. Only Chronicles says where the hired forces camped, before Medeba, and that the Ammonites gathered from their cities.

decisions.choice: Medeba: a town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: Medeba lay about twenty miles southwest of Rabbah, Ammon's capital, on the high plain north of the Arnon (Numbers 21:30; Joshua 13:9, 16). The hired army camped there, at a distance from the Ammonites, which fits the two separate battle lines of verse 9.

decisions.choice: his people: his army
decisions.reason: "People" here means the fighting men the king of Maacah led.

decisions.choice: his people (Literal); his army (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "people" means in a list of hired forces.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּשְׁלַח֙ אֶת־יוֹאָ֔ב וְאֵ֥ת כָּל־צָבָ֖א הַגִּבּוֹרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And heard David, and he sent Joab and all [the] army, the mighty men.

en.L: And David heard, and he sent Joab and all [the] army, the mighty men.
en.B: When David heard about this, he sent out Joab with the whole army of warriors.
en.R: When David heard about this, he sent out Joab with the whole army of fighting men.

decisions.choice: all the army, the mighty men: the whole army, all of them warriors
alternatives: the whole army and the mighty men (David's elite band)
decisions.reason: The two phrases stand side by side with no "and", as in 2 Samuel 10:7, where "army" has the article; here it does not. They are read here as one group, the army described as fighting men. They may also name two groups, the army and David's band of elite warriors (11:10-47).

decisions.choice: Joab: commander of David's army
decisions.reason: Joab was the son of David's sister Zeruiah (2:16) and commanded the army (11:6; 18:15).

decisions.choice: warriors (Balanced); fighting men (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word means strong men proven in battle. Literal keeps the traditional "mighty men", as in 2 Samuel 10:7.

source.text: וַיֵּצְאוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן וַיַּֽעַרְכ֥וּ מִלְחָמָ֖ה פֶּ֣תַח הָעִ֑יר וְהַמְּלָכִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֔אוּ לְבַדָּ֖ם בַּשָּׂדֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And came out [the] sons of Ammon and drew up battle [at the] entrance of the city, and the kings who had come [were] by themselves in the field.

en.L: And the sons of Ammon came out and drew up [for] battle at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come [were] by themselves in the field.
en.B: The Ammonites marched out and formed their battle line at the city entrance, while the kings who had come took a separate position in the open country.
en.R: The Ammonites marched out and got ready for battle at the entrance to their city. The kings who had come to help them took their places away from them, out in the open country.

decisions.choice: the entrance of the city and the kings who had come: differences from 2 Samuel 10:8
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:8 says "the entrance of the gate" and lists the allies again: the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob, and the men of Tob and Maacah. Chronicles says "the entrance of the city" and speaks only of "the kings who had come".

decisions.choice: by themselves in the field: as a separate force in the open country
decisions.reason: The hired forces did not stand with the Ammonites but took up a position of their own in open ground. That placed Joab's army between two enemy forces (verse 10).

decisions.choice: the city: most likely Rabbah, Ammon's capital
decisions.reason: The Ammonites stayed close to the walls of a city where they could retreat if beaten (verse 15). In 2 Samuel 10 and 11 this is Rabbah. Since Chronicles has just named Medeba (verse 7), the city could also be Medeba, but the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: the kings who had come to help them; their city
decisions.reason: Readable says why the kings had come and whose city it was, which the context makes clear.

source.text: וַיַּ֣רְא יוֹאָ֗ב כִּֽי־הָיְתָ֧ה פְנֵי־הַמִּלְחָמָ֛ה אֵלָ֖יו פָּנִ֣ים וְאָח֑וֹר וַיִּבְחַ֗ר מִכָּל־בָּחוּר֙ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַֽיַּעֲרֹ֖ךְ לִקְרַ֥את אֲרָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And saw Joab that was [the] face of the battle against him front and rear, and he chose from every chosen [man] in Israel and drew up to meet Aram.

en.L: And Joab saw that the front of the battle was against him in front and behind, and he chose from every chosen [man] in Israel and drew [them] up to meet Aram.
en.B: Joab saw that the battle lines faced him both in front and behind. So he picked some of Israel's best troops and lined them up against the Arameans.
en.R: Joab saw that he would have to fight enemies in front of him and enemies behind him. So he chose the best of Israel's soldiers and put them in place to fight the Arameans.

decisions.choice: the face of the battle was against him front and rear: he was facing enemy lines on two sides
decisions.reason: "The face of the battle" is the front line of an army. Joab found the Ammonites before the city on one side and the hired kings in the open country on the other (verse 9).

decisions.choice: every chosen man in Israel: compare 2 Samuel 10:9
decisions.reason: Chronicles says "from every chosen man in Israel". In 2 Samuel 10:9 the written consonants read "from all the chosen men in Israel" and the traditional reading in the margin has "of Israel". Samuel also says "from in front and from behind" where Chronicles has "front and rear". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: he chose from every chosen man: picked troops from the best
decisions.reason: The verb "chose" and the noun "chosen man" come from the same root. Joab took the best of Israel's soldiers to face the stronger enemy himself.

decisions.choice: Aram (Literal); the Arameans (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The land's name stands for its army. Balanced and Readable name the people, as in the rest of the chapter.

source.text: וְאֵת֙ יֶ֣תֶר הָעָ֔ם נָתַ֕ן בְּיַ֖ד אַבְשַׁ֣י אָחִ֑יו וַיַּ֣עַרְכ֔וּ לִקְרַ֖את בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of the people he gave into [the] hand of Abishai his brother, and they drew up to meet [the] sons of Ammon.

en.L: And the rest of the people he gave into [the] hand of Abishai his brother, and they drew up to meet the sons of Ammon.
en.B: He put the rest of the troops under the command of his brother Abishai, and they lined up against the Ammonites.
en.R: He put his brother Abishai in charge of the rest of the army. They lined up to face the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: gave into the hand of Abishai: put under Abishai's command
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for authority and control. Abishai was Joab's brother, another son of Zeruiah (2:16).

decisions.choice: they drew up: 2 Samuel 10:10 has "he drew up"
decisions.reason: In Samuel the verb is singular and may mean Joab or Abishai. Chronicles has the plural: Abishai's troops took up their positions facing the Ammonites.

decisions.choice: the people (Literal); the troops (Balanced); the army (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word "people" here means the fighting men in the field, as in 2 Samuel 10:10.

source.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אִם־תֶּחֱזַ֤ק מִמֶּ֨נִּי֙ אֲרָ֔ם וְהָיִ֥יתָ לִּ֖י לִתְשׁוּעָ֑הסוְאִם־בְּנֵ֥י עַמּ֛וֹן יֶֽחֶזְק֥וּ מִמְּךָ֖ וְהוֹשַׁעְתִּֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, If is too strong Aram for me, then you will be for me for help; and if [the] sons of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will help you.

en.L: And he said, "If Aram is too strong for me, then you shall be a help to me; and if the sons of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will help you.
en.B: Joab said, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, you must come to my rescue. But if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will rescue you.
en.R: Joab told Abishai, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, come and help me. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will help you.

decisions.choice: help, I will help you: rescue in battle
decisions.reason: The noun and the verb both come from the root that means to save or deliver. Here they mean coming to the aid of a fellow commander who is being overpowered, not salvation in a spiritual sense.

decisions.choice: too strong for me: stronger than the force I have
decisions.reason: The verb means "be strong"; with "for me" it means to overpower someone. Each brother promises to come to the other's side if his part of the battle goes badly.

decisions.choice: I will help you: 2 Samuel 10:11 has "I will come to help you"
decisions.reason: Chronicles has the verb "help" alone, without "come". The promise is the same.

decisions.choice: Joab said (Balanced); Joab told Abishai (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he said". Balanced names the speaker, and Readable also names the one he spoke to, as in 2 Samuel 10:11.

decisions.choice: help (Literal, Readable); rescue (Balanced)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "rescue" to keep the strength of the word; Literal and Readable say "help". Since the word here means aid in battle, "save" would mislead.

source.text: חֲזַ֤ק וְנִֽתְחַזְּקָה֙ בְּעַד־עַמֵּ֔נוּ וּבְעַ֖ד עָרֵ֣י אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ וַֽיהוָ֔ה הַטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינָ֖יו יַעֲשֶֽׂה׃

records.literal_gloss: Be strong, and let us show ourselves strong for our people and for [the] cities of our God; and Yahweh the good in his eyes will do.

en.L: Be strong, and let us show ourselves strong for our people and for the cities of our God; and may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do what is good in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes."
en.B: Be strong! Let us show courage for the sake of our people and the cities of our God. And may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do what seems good to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."
en.R: Be brave! Let us fight hard to protect our people and the cities of our God. And may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do whatever {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} thinks is best."

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Samuel 10:12
decisions.reason: Joab's call is word for word as in Samuel, except that the last clause puts "what is good in his eyes" before the verb "do". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: be strong, and let us show ourselves strong: an order and a shared call
decisions.reason: Joab first tells Abishai to be strong, then joins himself to the call: "let us". The second verb means to take courage and act boldly.

decisions.choice: the cities of our God: Israel's towns as belonging to God
decisions.reason: The towns of Israel stood in the land God had given his people. Defending them was defending what was his.

decisions.choice: may Yahweh do what is good in his eyes: a statement of trust that leaves the outcome to God
alternatives: and Yahweh will do what is good in his eyes
decisions.reason: The verb can be read as a wish ("may Yahweh do") or as a statement ("Yahweh will do"). Either way Joab commits the result of the battle to Yahweh after doing all he can (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26).

decisions.choice: let us show courage (Balanced); let us fight hard (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb means to show strength. Balanced says it is courage; Readable, in a battle speech, says what that strength is for. The wording follows 2 Samuel 10:12.

decisions.choice: what seems good to him (Balanced); whatever he thinks is best (Readable)
decisions.reason: "In his eyes" means "in his judgment". Literal keeps the picture.

source.text: וַיִּגַּ֨שׁ יוֹאָ֜ב וְהָעָ֧ם אֲשֶׁר־עִמּ֛וֹ לִפְנֵ֥י אֲרָ֖ם לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה וַיָּנ֖וּסוּ מִפָּנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And drew near Joab and the people who [were] with him before Aram for the battle, and they fled from before him.

en.L: And Joab and the people who [were] with him drew near before Aram for battle, and they fled before him.
en.B: Then Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans fled from him.
en.R: Then Joab and his soldiers moved forward to attack the Arameans, and the Arameans ran away from them.

decisions.choice: they fled before him: the Arameans ran from Joab
decisions.reason: "They" are the Arameans, and "him" is Joab. The hired army gave way as soon as Joab's picked troops attacked.

decisions.choice: before Aram: 2 Samuel 10:13 has "against Aram"
decisions.reason: Chronicles says Joab drew near "before" the Arameans for battle, where Samuel says he drew near to fight "against" them. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: the Arameans fled
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the ones who fled, which the Hebrew leaves to the context.

decisions.choice: the people (Literal); the troops (Balanced); his soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 11, "people" means the fighting men.

source.text: וּבְנֵ֨י עַמּ֤וֹן רָאוּ֙ כִּי־נָ֣ס אֲרָ֔ם וַיָּנ֣וּסוּ גַם־הֵ֗ם מִפְּנֵי֙ אַבְשַׁ֣י אָחִ֔יו וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ הָעִ֑ירָה וַיָּבֹ֥א יוֹאָ֖ב יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And [the] sons of Ammon saw that had fled Aram, and fled also they from before Abishai his brother and went into the city; and came Joab [to] Jerusalem.

en.L: And the sons of Ammon saw that Aram had fled, and they also fled before Abishai his brother and went into the city. And Joab came [to] Jerusalem.
en.B: When the Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, they also fled from Joab's brother Abishai and withdrew into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.
en.R: When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had run away, they also ran away from Abishai, Joab's brother, and went back into their city. So Joab went home to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 10:14
decisions.reason: Chronicles adds "also" and "his brother". Where Samuel says "Joab returned from fighting the sons of Ammon and came to Jerusalem", Chronicles says only "Joab came to Jerusalem".

decisions.choice: they went into the city, and Joab went to Jerusalem: a victory, but not yet a conquest
decisions.reason: The Ammonites were safe behind their city walls, and Joab did not stay to besiege it. The siege of Rabbah came the next spring (20:1-3).

decisions.choice: his brother: Joab's brother
decisions.reason: "His" refers back to Joab, who is named in verse 14 and again at the end of this verse.

decisions.choice: Joab's brother
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Joab, since "his brother" could otherwise seem to point to someone in this verse.

source.text: וַיַּ֣רְא אֲרָ֗ם כִּ֣י נִגְּפוּ֮ לִפְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וַֽיִּשְׁלְחוּ֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים וַיּוֹצִ֣יאוּ אֶת־אֲרָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֖ר מֵעֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר וְשׁוֹפַ֛ךְ שַׂר־צְבָ֥א הֲדַדְעֶ֖זֶר לִפְנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And saw Aram that they had been defeated before Israel, and they sent messengers and brought out Aram which [was] from beyond the River; and Shophach commander of [the] army of Hadadezer [was] before them.

en.L: And Aram saw that they had been defeated before Israel, and they sent messengers and brought out the Arameans who [were] beyond the River; and Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer [was] before them.
en.B: When the Arameans saw that they had been beaten by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Arameans who were beyond the Euphrates River, with Shophach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, at their head.
en.R: The Arameans saw that Israel had beaten them. So they sent messengers to bring more Arameans from the other side of the Euphrates River. Shophach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, led them.

decisions.choice: a shorter form of 2 Samuel 10:15-16, with the name Shophach
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 10:15-16 says the Arameans gathered together, that Hadadezer sent and brought out the Arameans beyond the River, and that they came to Helam. Chronicles says the defeated Arameans themselves sent messengers, and does not name Helam. Samuel spells the commander's name Shobach; Chronicles has Shophach. The two forms are the same name spelled differently.

decisions.choice: defeated: struck down in battle
decisions.reason: The verb means to be struck, and is used of an army routed by its enemy (1 Samuel 4:2, 10).

decisions.choice: the River: the Euphrates
decisions.reason: "The River" with no other name means the Euphrates (Genesis 31:21; Joshua 24:2). The Arameans living on its far side were under Hadadezer's power (18:3).

decisions.choice: Hadadezer: the king of Zobah of chapter 18
decisions.reason: Hadadezer was the strongest Aramean ruler of the time (18:3-8). Chapter 18 sums up David's victory over him, and this chapter tells how that war began.

decisions.choice: the Euphrates River; more Arameans (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the river, which the Hebrew calls simply "the River". Readable says "more Arameans", since these were fresh troops called up after the first defeat.

source.text: וַיֻּגַּ֣ד לְדָוִ֗יד וַיֶּאֱסֹ֤ף אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וַיַּעֲבֹ֣ר הַיַּרְדֵּ֔ן וַיָּבֹ֣א אֲלֵהֶ֔ם וַֽיַּעֲרֹ֖ךְ אֲלֵהֶ֑ם וַיַּעֲרֹ֨ךְ דָּוִ֜יד לִקְרַ֤את אֲרָם֙ מִלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּֽלָּחֲמ֖וּ עִמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was told to David, and he gathered all Israel and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up against them; and drew up David to meet Aram [for] battle, and they fought with him.

en.L: And it was told to David, and he gathered all Israel and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up against them. And David drew up [for] battle to meet Aram, and they fought with him.
en.B: When David was told, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, came up to them, and formed his lines against them. David drew up his army for battle against the Arameans, and they fought with him.
en.R: When David heard about it, he called together all the fighting men of Israel. They crossed the Jordan River and marched up to the Arameans and got into battle lines facing them. When David's army was ready for battle, the Arameans fought against him.

decisions.choice: David came to them and drew up: 2 Samuel 10:17 has "came to Helam" and "Aram drew up"
decisions.reason: Samuel says David came to Helam and the Arameans drew up their lines to meet him. Chronicles does not name the place, says David came "to them", and makes David the one who draws up the battle lines, twice over. Both books end the same way: the Arameans fought with him.

decisions.choice: all Israel: the whole fighting force of the nation
decisions.reason: This time David calls up the full army and leads it himself, because the Arameans have brought fresh forces from beyond the Euphrates.

decisions.choice: drew up against them, and David drew up: the same act told twice
decisions.reason: The second clause repeats the first and names David, making clear who set the battle in order before the fighting began.

decisions.choice: all the fighting men of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable says who "all Israel" were in a battle story: the men who could fight, as in 2 Samuel 10:17.

source.text: וַיָּ֣נָס אֲרָם֮ מִלִּפְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וַיַּהֲרֹ֨ג דָּוִ֜יד מֵאֲרָ֗ם שִׁבְעַ֤ת אֲלָפִים֙ רֶ֔כֶב וְאַרְבָּעִ֥ים אֶ֖לֶף אִ֣ישׁ רַגְלִ֑י וְאֵ֛ת שׁוֹפַ֥ךְ שַֽׂר־הַצָּבָ֖א הֵמִֽית׃

records.literal_gloss: And fled Aram from before Israel, and killed David of Aram seven thousand chariot[s] and forty thousand men on foot; and Shophach commander of the army he put to death.

en.L: And Aram fled before Israel, and David killed of Aram [the men of] 7,000 chariots and 40,000 men on foot; and he put to death Shophach the commander of the army.
en.B: But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed 7,000 of their charioteers and 40,000 foot soldiers. He also put to death Shophach, the commander of their army.
en.R: But the Arameans ran away from the Israelites. David and his army killed 7,000 Aramean soldiers who fought from chariots and 40,000 soldiers on foot. They also killed Shophach, the commander of the Aramean army.

decisions.choice: 7,000 chariot men and 40,000 foot soldiers: 2 Samuel 10:18 has 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen
decisions.reason: Samuel has seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen; Chronicles has seven thousand chariot men and forty thousand men on foot. Numbers were easily miscopied, and either book may have kept the original figure. The word for "thousand" may also name a military unit, as noted at Numbers 1, which would make the forces smaller.

decisions.choice: chariots: the men who fought from them
decisions.reason: The word means chariots or chariotry. Since David "killed" them, the sense is the crews of the chariots.

decisions.choice: David killed: David's army, led by the king
decisions.reason: As often in battle reports, the king is named for the army he leads (18:1-5).

decisions.choice: he put Shophach to death: killed in the battle or afterward
decisions.reason: The verb means "caused to die" and does not say whether Shophach fell in the fighting or was executed after it. 2 Samuel 10:18 says David struck him down and he died there.

decisions.choice: David and his army
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that David did not kill them alone, as in 2 Samuel 10:18.

decisions.choice: [the men of] 7,000 chariots (Literal); 7,000 charioteers (Balanced); soldiers who fought from chariots (Readable)
decisions.reason: The levels say that the men were killed, which is what the word means here.

source.text: וַיִּרְא֞וּ עַבְדֵ֣י הֲדַדְעֶ֗זֶר כִּ֤י נִגְּפוּ֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיַּשְׁלִ֥ימוּ עִם־דָּוִ֖יד וַיַּֽעַבְדֻ֑הוּ וְלֹא־אָבָ֣ה אֲרָ֔ם לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ אֶת־בְּנֵי־עַמּ֖וֹן עֽוֹד׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And saw [the] servants of Hadadezer that they had been defeated before Israel, and they made peace with David and served him; and not was willing Aram to help [the] sons of Ammon again.

en.L: And the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated before Israel, and they made peace with David and served him. And Aram was not willing to help the sons of Ammon anymore.
en.B: When those who were subject to Hadadezer saw that Israel had defeated them, they made peace with David and became his subjects. After this the Arameans were not willing to give the Ammonites any more help.
en.R: The people who had served Hadadezer saw that Israel had beaten them. So they made peace with David and served him instead. After that, the Arameans would not help the Ammonites again.

decisions.choice: the servants of Hadadezer: rulers and peoples bound to serve him
decisions.reason: Here "servants" names those who owed loyalty and tribute to Hadadezer as their overlord; 2 Samuel 10:19 calls them "all the kings, the servants of Hadadezer". After the battle they owed the same service to David.

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 10:19
decisions.reason: Samuel says "all the kings" made peace "with Israel" and served "them", and that Aram "was afraid" to help Ammon any more. Chronicles has "the servants of Hadadezer", says they made peace "with David" and served "him", and says Aram "was not willing" to help.

decisions.choice: Ammon left to fight alone
decisions.reason: With its allies gone, Ammon now faced David by itself. The story goes on in 20:1, when Joab besieges Rabbah.

decisions.choice: servants (Literal); those who were subject to (Balanced); the people who had served (Readable)
decisions.reason: These "servants" are subject rulers and peoples, not officials or envoys, so Balanced and Readable describe their position instead.
